The instruction is simple, almost disarmingly so: write whatever comes to you. No prompt, no constraint, no hidden agenda—just a blank space and a thousand words to fill. The moment I read it, my mind goes blank, which is always the way. It’s like standing in an empty room and being told to make a noise. Any noise. The possibilities are so vast that they collapse into a single, silent point.

So I begin with the beginning—with the feel of the keyboard under my fingers, the soft clack of keys, the glow of the screen. I’m sitting in a chair that creaks if I lean too far back. The window is to my left, half-open, letting in the smell of rain that hasn’t quite decided to fall. The sky is a colorless grey, the kind that makes time feel slower, as if the afternoon is holding its breath. Somewhere outside, a dog barks once, twice, then stops. A car passes, its tires hissing on the damp asphalt. These are the small details that make up a life, the quiet texture of an ordinary day.

I think about how strange it is to be alive at this particular moment in history. I can sit here and type words that will be read—maybe—by a person I’ve never met, on a screen that exists somewhere else entirely, at a time that might be weeks or years from now. The words are just marks, little symbols, but they carry meaning, emotion, intention. They are a bridge. And yet, they are also a cage. Every word I choose narrows the infinite field of what I could say. To write is to choose, and to choose is to lose the other options. But it’s also to make something real, to pull a thread of thought from the chaos and hold it up to the light.

Lately I’ve been thinking about memory. Not the grand, historical kind, but the small, personal kind. The way a smell can transport you back to a kitchen you haven’t seen in twenty years. The way a song can make your chest ache with a longing you can’t quite name. I remember a summer evening when I was a child, catching fireflies in a mason jar. The jar had a metal lid with holes punched in it, and the fireflies blinked like tiny, angry stars. I didn’t understand then why they glowed. I just knew it was magic. Now I know it’s chemistry—luciferin, luciferase, oxygen, ATP. But knowing the mechanism doesn’t dim the magic. If anything, it deepens it. The fact that a small beetle can produce light from a chemical reaction, that this light exists only to attract a mate, that I, a mammal with opposable thumbs, can witness it and feel wonder—that is a kind of poetry that science can’t erase.

I think about the people I’ve loved and lost. Not to death, mostly, but to time and distance. There are friends from high school whose faces I can still see clearly, whose voices I can almost hear, but who are now strangers. We share a past, but no present. Is that a kind of death? Or is it something gentler, like a book that closes and sits on a shelf, unread but not forgotten? I used to think that relationships were permanent, that once you connected with someone, the thread was unbreakable. But threads can fray. They can be cut. And sometimes they simply dissolve, like sugar in water, until you can’t tell where you end and they begin, and then you realize you’ve become two separate people again, and you don’t know when it happened.

There’s a philosophy that says you can never step into the same river twice. Heraclitus said that. The water is always different, and so are you. I think about that when I revisit places from my childhood. The house where I grew up has been repainted. The tree I used to climb has been cut down. The street feels wider, the sidewalk shorter. But the strangest thing isn’t that the place changed—it’s that I expected it to be the same. I expected to walk in and find my twelve-year-old self still there, waiting for me. But of course, she’s gone. She’s me, but not me. She lives only in photographs and in the scattered, unreliable archives of memory.

I wonder if this is what it means to be human: to be a time traveler who can only move forward, but who spends half their life looking back. We are made of stories—the ones we tell ourselves, the ones we tell others, the ones we refuse to tell. Every person has a narrative, a thread winding through the labyrinth of their days. And every narrative is full of gaps, ellipses, moments we edit out because they’re too painful or too boring or too confusing to include. The story of a life is never the whole story. It’s a highlight reel, a curated selection, a series of scenes stitched together to make some kind of sense.

I think about language itself. The fact that I can write “I think about language itself” and you can read it and understand it is, frankly, miraculous. Words are arbitrary sounds and shapes, agreed upon by millions of people over thousands of years, passed down like stones from hand to hand. They are older than us, and they will be older still. The word “tree” is not a tree. The word “love” is not love. But somehow, by arranging these symbols, I can make you feel something. I can make you remember your own summer evenings, your own lost friends, your own quiet grey afternoons. That is the closest thing to magic I know.

And yet, language is also a wall. It is a way to hide. We say “I’m fine” when we’re falling apart. We say “goodbye” when we mean “please don’t leave.” We write emails that are polite masks, text messages that are arrows. The same tool that connects us can keep us at arm’s length. To write honestly is to risk being known, and being known is terrifying. So we hide behind irony, behind wit, behind facts and figures and small talk. We craft our sentences like armor. But every once in a while, we let the armor drop. We write a poem. We hold someone’s hand. We say, out loud, the thing we’ve been carrying in our chest for years. And the word that comes out is small and fragile, like a firefly in a jar. But it glows.

I don’t know where this is going. I’m following the current of my own mind, letting one thought lead to the next. That’s what “whatever comes to you” means, I suppose. It means trusting the process, trusting that your brain will find its way, that the tangled knot of your thoughts has a loose end somewhere. And it does. It always does. You just have to start pulling.

I think about the future. Not the grand, historical future, but my future. Where will I be in ten years? Twenty? Will I still be writing? Will I still be the same person who started this paragraph? The self is a strange thing—always the same, always changing. We are a river and a stone, a flame and the ash it leaves behind. I don’t know what I’ll become. But I know that I’m here, now, at this keyboard, with a thousand words and the freedom to use them any way I like. That is enough. That is, in fact, everything.

So I’ll end where I began: with the simple fact of writing. The words are not perfect. They never are. But they are mine, for this moment, and then they are yours. Read them, or don’t. The act of writing is its own reward. The act of reading is another. We are connected, you and I, across the strange bridge of language. And for that, I am grateful.

The sky is still grey. The rain has started to fall, a soft patter against the window. The dog barks again, a little farther away now. The afternoon is moving on. And I am here, in this moment, with the quiet hum of the computer and the gentle blur of words. It is an ordinary moment. It is a miracle. Both are true. And that is all I have, and all I need.
